intro: Martial arts and combat sports do not live only in private schools. Armies taught them in training camps. Colleges built teams around them. Public schools in Japan, Okinawa and Illinois put them into the school day, often for a few weeks at a time. Each of these places changed the art to fit its own clock, its own goals and its own rules.

In this unit you will follow those changes with dates and documents. You will meet the 1917 camp boxing program, Yosh Uchida's judo team at San Jose State and Itosu Ankō's karate classes in Shuri. You will read the New York boxing laws of 1896, 1911 and 1920, the Lystedt Law of 2009 and Illinois's concussion laws. You will also see how Title IX and the Paralympic Games opened doors.

By the end, you will be able to explain who regulates a training room and a competition. You will compare a short school unit with a long teaching lineage. You will name the laws, agencies and governing bodies that answer when someone gets hurt, and say when each one began.
bigQuestion: When armies, schools and states take up a martial art, what do they keep, what do they leave out and who becomes responsible for safety?

title: What PE Flattens

chapters.title: Martial Arts in School and Service
chapters.bigQuestion: What happens to an old martial art when an army, a college or a school day gives it only a few weeks?

story.title: Six Weeks for Six Centuries
story.kicker: A new PE unit plan sits on a desk beside a family scroll that took a lifetime to earn.
paragraphs: Ms. Ortega teaches physical education at a high school in central Illinois. In August her department hands her a new plan. It gives her a six-week unit called Martial Arts and Self-Defense. The plan fits between volleyball and a fitness test. Each class meets for forty-seven minutes.

A student named Daniel stays after class on the first day. His grandfather trains in a Japanese sword school near Chiba. That school's own records trace it to the 1400s. Daniel shows a photo of a paper license scroll on his phone. The scroll lists teachers' names going back many generations.

Ms. Ortega looks at her plan again. The district office has added a page of forms. There is a parent permission slip, a note about insurance and a rule that any guest teacher must pass a background check. The plan also says students will study where the arts came from.

"Six weeks," Daniel says, "for something that took six hundred years." Ms. Ortega does not argue. She starts a list on the board. It asks who first carried these arts into armies, colleges and school gyms, and what each one had to leave out.
story.think: What can a six-week school unit do well, and what might it leave out of a tradition that is centuries old?

lessons.title: Boxing in the Camps of 1917
lessons.mainIdea: During World War I, the U.S. War Department used boxing in training camps, and many soldiers came home knowing the sport.
reading: The United States entered World War I in April 1917. Within weeks, Secretary of War Newton D. Baker created the *Commission on Training Camp Activities*. Raymond Fosdick led it. Its job was to fill soldiers' free hours in the new camps. The commission brought in sports, libraries, singing and theater.

Boxing became one of the largest camp sports. In 1917 prize fighting for money was illegal or limited in many states. In the camps, boxing was run as training and recreation, not as a paid show. Officers saw the sport as a way to build fitness and team spirit. Thousands of young men put on gloves for the first time.

The most famous example is Gene Tunney. He served in the U.S. Marine Corps in France. In 1919 he won the light heavyweight title of the American Expeditionary Forces, the U.S. Army in Europe. In 1926 he became heavyweight champion of the world. Camp boxing helped make the sport more respectable, and several states legalized professional bouts in the early 1920s.

words.d: a U.S. War Department body created in 1917 to organize sports and recreation for soldiers in training camps
the U.S. Army sent to Europe during World War I
boxing for a cash prize; illegal or limited in many U.S. states before the 1920s

look.title: A Camp Bulletin, 1918
look.text: Picture a notice board in an Army training camp in 1918. One sheet lists a Tuesday boxing class. Another lists a Friday night bout card between two companies. A third announces a library tent and a singing night. All three sheets carry the same stamp from the camp's recreation office.
look.prompt: Why might the Army put boxing on the same board as a library and a singing night?

choices: Secretary of War Newton D. Baker
check.why: Newton D. Baker set up the commission soon after the U.S. entered World War I, with Raymond Fosdick in charge.

check.q: How was boxing in the 1917 camps different from prize fighting?
choices: It was held only in France.
It was run as training and recreation, not as a paid show.

check.why: Camp boxing was part of training and recreation, while prize fighting paid cash prizes and was limited in many states.

check.q: What title did Gene Tunney win in 1919?
choices: the light heavyweight title of the American Expeditionary Forces
check.why: Tunney, a Marine, won the AEF light heavyweight title in 1919 and later became world heavyweight champion in 1926.

lessons.title: Combatives in World War II
lessons.mainIdea: In World War II, armies taught short combatives courses that borrowed from boxing, wrestling and jujutsu but left the older traditions behind.
reading: *Combatives* is the military word for close hand-to-hand fighting taught to troops. The word names a course, not one art. In World War II, armies needed to train millions of people fast. A combatives course often lasted only days or a few weeks. It had no belts, no bowing and no lineage of teachers.

Two British men shaped many of these courses. William E. Fairbairn and Eric A. Sykes had served in the Shanghai Municipal Police in China. Fairbairn joined that force in 1907. In Shanghai they studied boxing, wrestling, jujutsu and Chinese arts. From 1940 they trained British commandos and agents of the Special Operations Executive.

Americans wrote their own manuals too. Anthony J. Drexel Biddle published Do or Die for the U.S. Marine Corps in 1937. Fairbairn published Get Tough! in 1942 and later trained agents of the U.S. Office of Strategic Services. Rex Applegate wrote Kill or Get Killed in 1943. Each book stripped arts down to what a soldier could learn quickly.

words.d: the military term for hand-to-hand fighting courses taught to troops
a British wartime agency, formed in 1940, that trained agents to work behind enemy lines
the U.S. wartime intelligence agency, formed in 1942, often called the OSS

look.prompt: Which manual appeared before the United States entered World War II in December 1941?

check.q: What does the military word combatives name?
choices: a course of hand-to-hand fighting taught to troops
check.why: Combatives is the military term for close-fighting courses, not the name of one traditional art.

check.q: Where did Fairbairn and Sykes serve before training British commandos?
check.why: Both men served in the Shanghai Municipal Police, where they studied several arts.

check.q: How did a wartime combatives course differ from a traditional school?
choices: It lasted many years and gave dan ranks.
It was short and had no belts or teacher lineage.
It was taught only to officers' children.
check.why: Wartime courses lasted days or weeks and dropped ranks, rituals and lineages to train many people fast.

lessons.title: Belts in the Marine Corps
lessons.mainIdea: After 1945, service members carried Asian arts home, and in 2001 the Marine Corps built its own belt system.
reading: Judo reached the U.S. military early. In 1905 the judo teacher Yamashita Yoshitsugu taught at the U.S. Naval Academy in Annapolis, Maryland. That same period, President Theodore Roosevelt trained with him at the White House. The Navy program was short, but it showed Americans a Kodokan teacher in person.

The bigger wave came after World War II. From 1945, the United States occupied Japan and ran Okinawa until 1972. U.S. troops also stayed in South Korea after the Korean War ended in 1953. Many service members trained in local judo, karate and taekwondo schools. Back home, some of them opened clubs in American towns.

In 2001 the U.S. Marine Corps started the *Marine Corps Martial Arts Program*, called MCMAP. It uses colored belts: tan, gray, green, brown and black, with degrees of black belt. Marines wear the belts on their uniforms. The program also teaches character and Marine Corps history. The Army published its own manual, FM 3-25.150, Combatives, in 2002.

words.d: the U.S. Marine Corps training system begun in 2001, with belts from tan to black
control of a country or territory by a foreign military; the U.S. occupied Japan after 1945 and governed Okinawa until 1972
an official U.S. Army training book, such as FM 3-25.150, Combatives, published in 2002

lessons.title: Yosh Uchida at San Jose State
lessons.mainIdea: Yosh Uchida built the San Jose State judo program after World War II, while his own family had been held in a wartime camp.
reading: Yoshihiro "Yosh" Uchida was born in California in 1920 to Japanese immigrant parents. He studied at San Jose State College and began helping with its judo club as a student. Then war came. On February 19, 1942, President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed *Executive Order 9066*.

The order led to the forced removal of about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry from the West Coast. Most were American citizens. They were held in camps the government called relocation centers. Uchida's family was among those removed. Uchida himself served in the U.S. Army during the war. In 1988 Congress passed the Civil Liberties Act, which apologized and paid survivors.

Uchida returned to San Jose State in 1946 and coached judo there for decades. He treated judo as a college sport with a team, a schedule and national titles. San Jose State later became the best-known college judo program in the country. In 1964 Uchida was head coach of the first U.S. Olympic judo team, at the Tokyo Games.

words.d: the 1942 order that led to the forced removal and detention of Japanese Americans on the West Coast
being held in confinement; historians use it for the wartime camps that held Japanese Americans
the 1988 U.S. law that apologized for the wartime incarceration and paid surviving Japanese Americans

look.title: The Order of February 19, 1942
look.text: The order let the Secretary of War and military commanders mark off military areas. From those areas, any person could be excluded. The order did not name any group, but it was used to remove Japanese Americans from the West Coast.
look.cite: Executive Order 9066, signed by President Franklin D. Roosevelt, February 19, 1942
look.prompt: The order named no group. How can a historian show whom it actually affected?

choices: the forced removal of Japanese Americans from the West Coast

check.why: The 1942 order led to the removal and detention of about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry.

check.q: When did Uchida return to coach judo at San Jose State?
check.why: After his Army service, Uchida returned to San Jose State in 1946.

check.q: What did the Civil Liberties Act of 1988 do?
choices: It made judo an NCAA sport.

lessons.title: Judo Joins the Olympic Program
lessons.mainIdea: Judo became an Olympic sport at Tokyo in 1964, which gave college programs a clear national and world goal.
reading: Most college sports in the United States are run by the *NCAA*, the National Collegiate Athletic Association, founded in 1906. Judo is not an NCAA championship sport. College judo teams compete through their own national collegiate association instead. This makes judo a club-level college sport at most schools.

The Olympic stage changed judo's weight in the world. Tokyo hosted the 1964 Summer Olympics, and judo was added for those Games. Kanō Jigorō had joined the International Olympic Committee in 1909. He was the first member from Asia. Judo reached the Olympics decades after his death in 1938.

At Tokyo in 1964, James Bregman won a bronze medal. It was the first Olympic judo medal for the United States. The Dutch athlete Anton Geesink won the open-weight gold, beating Japan's Kaminaga Akio. Judo was left out of the 1968 Games in Mexico City. It returned in 1972 at Munich and has stayed on the program.

words.d: the National Collegiate Athletic Association, founded in 1906, which runs most U.S. college championships
the body that runs the Olympic Games; Kanō Jigorō joined it in 1909
a judo division with no weight limit, held at the 1964 Olympics

check.why: Kanō Jigorō joined the International Olympic Committee in 1909 as its first Asian member.

check.q: Which Games did NOT include judo?
check.why: Judo debuted in 1964, was dropped for Mexico City in 1968 and returned in 1972.

check.q: Who won the first U.S. Olympic judo medal?
check.why: James Bregman won bronze at Tokyo in 1964, the first U.S. Olympic judo medal.

lessons.title: Doors That Opened Late
lessons.mainIdea: Women and athletes with disabilities were kept out of judo competition for decades, and people and laws opened those doors.
reading: In 1959 Rena "Rusty" Kanokogi of Brooklyn won a YMCA judo tournament in upstate New York. She had entered on a team of men. Officials asked for her medal back because she was a woman. She spent the next decades pushing for women's judo. In 1980 she organized the first women's world judo championships, held at Madison Square Garden in New York.

U.S. law changed at the same time. *Title IX* of the Education Amendments of 1972 bans sex discrimination in school programs that receive federal money. Colleges and high schools had to open more teams to women. Women's judo was a demonstration event at the 1988 Seoul Olympics. It became a full medal event at Barcelona in 1992.

Judo also opened to blind and visually impaired athletes. It joined the *Paralympic Games* at Seoul in 1988, for men. Women's Paralympic judo followed at Athens in 2004. The International Blind Sports Federation governs the sport. Paralympic judo shows that one art can hold more than one kind of athlete.

words.d: part of the Education Amendments of 1972 that bans sex discrimination in federally funded school programs
a sport shown at the Olympics without official medals
the international games for athletes with disabilities, held after each Olympics

look.title: The Words of Title IX
look.text: No person in the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance.
look.cite: Title IX, Education Amendments of 1972, 20 U.S.C. 1681(a)
look.prompt: Title IX never names judo or any sport. Why does it still reach a college judo team?

check.q: Why was Rusty Kanokogi asked to return her medal in 1959?
choices: She had used a banned rule book.
She was a woman on a men's team.
check.why: Officials took back her YMCA medal because she was a woman competing on a men's team.

check.q: When did women's judo become a full Olympic medal event?
check.why: Women's judo was a demonstration in 1988 and became a medal event at Barcelona in 1992.

check.q: What does Title IX ban?
choices: sex discrimination in federally funded school programs
check.why: Title IX bans sex discrimination in education programs that receive federal money.

lessons.title: Judo and Kendo in Japanese Schools
lessons.mainIdea: Japan put judo and kendo into its schools, banned them after 1945 and later required martial arts in junior high PE again.
reading: Kanō Jigorō was an educator as well as judo's founder. For many years he led the Tokyo Higher Normal School, which trained teachers. He argued that judo belonged in education. In 1911 Japan's Ministry of Education added judo and *kendo*, the sport of bamboo swords, to the middle-school course of study.

In the 1930s and early 1940s, Japan's government tied school martial arts to military training. After Japan's defeat in 1945, the Allied occupation ended martial arts in schools. In 1946 it also dissolved the *Dai Nippon Butoku Kai*, a national martial arts society founded in Kyoto in 1895. Judo returned to schools in 1950 as a sport, and kendo followed in the early 1950s.

A newer change came in 2012. Japan's national course of study began requiring budo, or martial arts, in the first two years of junior high PE. Schools choose which art to offer, such as judo, kendo or sumo. The change led to a public debate about safety. News reports described student deaths and serious injuries in school judo in past decades, and teacher training was expanded.

words.d: the Japanese sport of fencing with bamboo swords and armor
a national Japanese martial arts society founded in Kyoto in 1895 and dissolved in 1946
a national list of what schools must teach; Japan's Ministry of Education sets it

Budo required in junior high PE
look.cite: Japan Ministry of Education course of study records
look.prompt: How long were martial arts out of Japanese schools after 1945 before judo returned?

check.q: Which school did Kanō Jigorō lead for many years?
check.why: Kanō led the Tokyo Higher Normal School, a college for training teachers.

check.q: What happened to the Dai Nippon Butoku Kai in 1946?
choices: It was dissolved during the Allied occupation.
check.why: The occupation dissolved the society, founded in Kyoto in 1895, in 1946.

check.q: What did Japan's 2012 course of study require?

lessons.title: Karate Enters Okinawan Schools
lessons.mainIdea: In 1901 Itosu Ankō brought karate into an Okinawan school, and in 1908 he wrote a letter asking officials to teach it more widely.
reading: Okinawa was once the center of the *Ryukyu Kingdom*. Japan annexed the kingdom and made it Okinawa Prefecture in 1879. Karate grew on Okinawa from local practice and Chinese arts. For a long time it was taught privately, often to a few students at a time.

Itosu Ankō was a karate teacher in Shuri, the old royal capital. In 1901 he began teaching karate at Shuri Jinjō Elementary School. Within a few years it was taught at the Okinawa Prefectural Middle School and the prefecture's teacher-training school. Itosu created new, simpler forms for school classes. Teaching dozens of children at once changed how karate was organized.

In 1908 Itosu wrote a letter to Okinawa's education officials. It is often called his ten precepts of karate. In it he argued that karate builds health and character in young people. He asked that it be taught in all Okinawan schools. The letter is one of the earliest written records about karate's purpose.

words.d: the island kingdom centered on Okinawa, annexed by Japan in 1879
a region of Japan with its own local government, like a state
a short rule or principle; Itosu wrote ten about karate in 1908

look.title: Itosu's Letter of 1908
look.text: Karate did not come from Buddhism or Confucianism. It can build strong bodies and steady character. It should be taught in schools so that young people grow healthy and are ready to serve.
look.cite: Itosu Ankō, letter to Okinawa Prefecture education officials (ten precepts of karate), 1908
look.prompt: Why would a teacher writing to school officials stress health and character?

check.q: When did Japan make the Ryukyu Kingdom into Okinawa Prefecture?
check.why: Japan annexed the Ryukyu Kingdom and made it Okinawa Prefecture in 1879.

check.q: Where did Itosu Ankō begin teaching karate in 1901?
choices: the Dai Nippon Butoku Kai in Kyoto
check.why: Itosu started karate classes at Shuri Jinjō Elementary School in 1901.

check.q: What did Itosu ask for in his 1908 letter?
choices: that karate be banned for children
that karate move to mainland China
that karate be taught in all Okinawan schools
check.why: His letter to education officials argued karate built health and character and asked for it in every school.

lessons.title: Units in an American Gym
lessons.mainIdea: In U.S. schools, martial arts usually appear as short PE units chosen by each district, while wrestling runs as a separate school sport.
reading: American states, not the federal government, set most school rules. Illinois law has long required physical education for students in every grade. The law does not name which activities a school must teach. Districts and teachers decide. A self-defense or martial arts unit is one choice among many.

National groups describe goals instead of sports. *SHAPE America*, the national organization for health and PE teachers, publishes national PE standards. They describe skills such as moving well, staying active and working safely with others. A school can meet those goals with dance, swimming, volleyball or a martial arts unit. That is why units differ so much between districts.

Wrestling follows a different path. In Illinois it is an interscholastic sport run by the Illinois High School Association, founded in 1900. Boys crowned their first IHSA state wrestling champions in 1937. Girls held their first IHSA state finals in 2022. A wrestling team has coaches, a season and a rule book, while a PE unit has a few weeks and a grade.

words.d: the national organization for health and physical education teachers; it publishes national PE standards
played between schools, such as an IHSA team sport
a block of lessons on one topic, often a few weeks long in PE

look.title: Two Plans on One Desk
look.text: Plan A is a six-week PE unit. It lists thirty class periods, a written quiz and a grade. Plan B is the wrestling team's season. It lists months of practice, a weigh-in schedule, IHSA regional dates and a state final. Both plans use the same mats in the same room.
look.prompt: Which plan answers to a statewide governing body, and which answers to the school district?

check.q: Who usually decides which activities a U.S. PE class teaches?
check.why: State law requires PE, but districts and teachers choose the activities.

check.q: What does SHAPE America publish?
check.why: SHAPE America publishes standards that describe PE goals instead of naming required sports.

check.q: When did Illinois girls hold their first IHSA state wrestling finals?
check.why: The IHSA held its first girls state wrestling finals in 2022; boys began in 1937.

lessons.title: A School Older Than the Gym
lessons.mainIdea: Some martial arts schools pass on authority through teachers and licenses over centuries, which no short unit can copy.
reading: In Japan, the oldest sword and weapons schools are called *koryu*, or "old schools." One is Tenshin Shōden Katori Shintō-ryū, in Chiba Prefecture near the Katori Shrine. The school's own tradition says Iizasa Chōisai Ienao founded it around 1447. It is still taught today by a line of headmasters.

Koryu schools often mark a student's progress with written licenses. The highest is often called *menkyo kaiden*, a license of full transmission. A scroll may list every headmaster back to the founder. Earning such a license can take decades. The school decides who may teach its name.

Judo kept part of this idea but changed its form. Kanō Jigorō studied Tenjin Shin'yō-ryū and Kitō-ryū jujutsu before founding the Kodokan in 1882. In 1883 he awarded the first dan ranks to two students, Tomita Tsunejirō and Saigō Shirō. Dan ranks gave one school a clear ladder that many people could climb.

words.d: "old school"; a Japanese martial tradition founded before the modern era, often before 1868
a license of full transmission, the highest written license in many koryu schools
a numbered black-belt rank; Kanō Jigorō first awarded dan ranks in 1883

look.title: A Scroll and a Report Card
look.text: On the left is a paper scroll from an old Japanese school. It lists names of teachers across many generations and ends with one student's name. On the right is a PE report card. It lists a six-week unit, a quiz score and a letter grade.
look.prompt: What does each document say about who has the right to teach?

check.q: What does koryu mean?
check.why: Koryu means old school, a Japanese tradition from before the modern era.

check.q: According to its own tradition, when was Katori Shintō-ryū founded?

lessons.title: Waivers, Insurance and the Law
lessons.mainIdea: Schools that offer martial arts must plan for injuries, insurance and the safety of minors under state and federal law.
reading: When a school adds a contact activity, it takes on legal duties. In law, *negligence* means failing to use reasonable care, which leads to harm. A school owes students supervision, safe equipment and trained staff. Courts ask whether a reasonable school would have done the same thing.

Illinois passed the Local Governmental and Governmental Employees Tort Immunity Act in 1965. It protects public bodies, including school districts, from many injury lawsuits. It has exceptions for conduct the law calls willful and wanton. Many districts also ask outside instructors to show *liability insurance* before they teach. Parents often sign a waiver, but courts in many states limit waivers signed for children.

Federal law added a safety layer for youth sport. The U.S. Center for SafeSport opened in Denver in 2017. The Safe Sport Authorization Act of 2017, signed into law in February 2018, gave the center federal authority. USA Judo, USA Taekwondo, USA Wrestling and USA Boxing must follow its rules on abuse prevention, reporting and training for adults who work with minors.

chapters.title: Who Regulates the Room
chapters.bigQuestion: When people train or compete in a combat sport, who makes the safety rules, and who answers when someone gets hurt?

story.title: A License by the Door
story.kicker: A framed state license hangs in a Chicago boxing gym, but it does not cover the room itself.
paragraphs: A boxing gym sits above a tire shop on Chicago's Southwest Side. A framed paper hangs beside its front door. It is a state license from the Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation. It says the owner, Mr. Reyes, may work as a second, the helper in a boxer's corner on fight night.

A high school junior named Aaliyah comes in to sign up. Her mother reads the license and asks a question. "So the state checked this gym?" Mr. Reyes shakes his head. The license covers him at a professional bout, he explains. The room itself only needs a city business license and a fire inspection.

Aaliyah wrestles for her school, too. Her team follows other rules. There are weigh-ins before each meet, and a referee checks every wrestler's skin. Last year a teammate hit her head and had to sit out. A form from a doctor was needed before she could return.

Aaliyah's mother takes a photo of the license. On the drive home, they count the rule makers they saw in one afternoon. There was the state, the city, the school, a doctor and a national rule book for high school wrestling. Each one watches a different part of the same sport.

lessons.title: Bare Knuckles and Gloves
lessons.mainIdea: In the late 1800s, boxing moved from outlawed bare-knuckle fights to gloved bouts under the Queensberry Rules.
reading: Older English boxing followed the *London Prize Ring Rules*, first written in 1838 and revised in 1853. Fighters used bare fists. A round ended only when a man went down, so fights could last hours. Most American states treated these fights as illegal. Promoters often held them in secret places to avoid the police.

In 1867 a new code was published in London. John Graham Chambers wrote it, and John Sholto Douglas, the ninth Marquess of Queensberry, lent his name. The *Queensberry Rules* required padded gloves and three-minute rounds with one minute of rest. A fighter who was down had ten seconds to rise. The code made boxing look more like a sport with a clock.

The change reached the heavyweight title in two famous fights. On July 8, 1889, John L. Sullivan beat Jake Kilrain in 75 rounds at Richburg, Mississippi. It was the last heavyweight title fight under bare-knuckle rules, and Sullivan was later prosecuted in Mississippi for taking part. On September 7, 1892, James J. Corbett beat Sullivan in New Orleans, wearing gloves under Queensberry rules.

the boxing code published in 1867 that required gloves and three-minute rounds
a person or company that organizes and sells tickets to a bout

lessons.title: New York Tries Three Laws
lessons.mainIdea: New York legalized boxing, banned it and legalized it again before the 1920 Walker Law made the change last.
reading: New York was the biggest boxing market in the United States. It also changed its mind several times. In 1896 the *Horton Law* allowed boxing matches run by athletic clubs. Critics said the bouts were brutal and tied to gambling. In 1900 the state repealed the law, and prize fighting was banned again.

In 1911 the *Frawley Law* opened the door partway. It allowed bouts of up to ten rounds. It also set up a state commission to watch over boxing. Official decisions were not allowed, so a bout ended with no winner declared. Newspaper writers often named the winner instead. The Frawley Law was repealed in 1917.

In 1920 the state passed the Walker Law. It legalized boxing with judges' decisions and bouts of up to fifteen rounds. It also created the New York State Athletic Commission. This time the law lasted. The three laws show how a state can test a new rule, reverse it and then try again with stronger supervision.

a New York law of 1911 that allowed ten-round bouts with no official decision; repealed in 1917
to cancel a law officially

lessons.title: What the Walker Law Built
lessons.mainIdea: The Walker Law made boxing a licensed trade, and other states, including Illinois, built similar systems.
reading: The Walker Law was named for state senator James J. Walker. He later served as mayor of New York City, starting in 1926. His law made boxing a *licensed* business. Boxers, managers, seconds, referees, judges and promoters all needed a license from the new *athletic commission*. The commission could suspend a license or hold back a purse.

The commission also required medical checks before bouts. A doctor had to examine each boxer. The commission set the number of rounds and approved each card of bouts. In this way, a state agency began watching the room on fight night. Other states soon set up their own commissions on the New York model.

Illinois legalized professional boxing in the 1920s. On September 22, 1927, Gene Tunney and Jack Dempsey fought at Soldier Field in Chicago before more than 100,000 people. Today the Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation licenses professional boxers and officials. It works under the state's Boxing and Full-contact Martial Arts Act.

holding official permission from the government to do a job

lessons.title: Fifteen Rounds Become Twelve
lessons.mainIdea: After Duk Koo Kim died following a 1982 title fight, major boxing organizations shortened championship bouts to twelve rounds.
reading: On November 13, 1982, Ray Mancini defended his lightweight title against Duk Koo Kim of South Korea. The bout took place outside Caesars Palace in Las Vegas, Nevada. It was scheduled for fifteen rounds. Kim was stopped in the fourteenth round and fell into a coma. He died four days later.

Professional titles are awarded by *sanctioning bodies*, private groups that rank boxers and approve title fights. The World Boxing Council, or WBC, was the first to act. Soon after Kim's death, it cut its title bouts from fifteen rounds to twelve. The World Boxing Association and the International Boxing Federation later made the same change.

The fight led to other changes too. Commissions paid more attention to medical exams before and after bouts. Kim's death also touched people far from the ring. His mother died by suicide a few months later, and the referee, Richard Green, died the next year. The story shows how one death can reshape a rule book.

a fight for a title, once scheduled for fifteen rounds and now for twelve

lessons.title: Congress Steps Into Boxing
lessons.mainIdea: In 1996 and 2000, Congress passed laws that set national floors for boxer safety and fair contracts.
reading: For most of the 1900s, only states regulated boxing. Rules varied from one state to the next. A boxer suspended in one state could sometimes fight in another. Promoters could move bouts to places with weak commissions or none at all. Reformers asked Congress to set a national floor.

Congress passed the *Professional Boxing Safety Act of 1996*. It said no professional bout may be held in the United States unless a state or tribal commission supervises it. It required a physical exam for each boxer and an ambulance and doctor at each bout. It also created a national identification card for professional boxers.

In 2000 Congress passed the *Muhammad Ali Boxing Reform Act*. Ali, the former heavyweight champion, lent his name to the effort. The law aimed to protect boxers from unfair contracts. It also required sanctioning bodies to make their ranking rules public. State and tribal commissions work together through the Association of Boxing Commissions.

a federal law of 2000 that aimed to protect boxers from unfair contracts and hidden rankings

lessons.title: Who Governs Olympic Boxing
lessons.mainIdea: Olympic boxing answers to an international federation, and in the 2020s the IOC replaced the old federation with a new one.
reading: Olympic boxing is amateur boxing. It follows different rules and bodies than professional bouts. Boxing first appeared at the Olympics at St. Louis in 1904. The *International Amateur Boxing Association*, known as AIBA, was founded in 1946 to govern the amateur sport worldwide. In the United States, USA Boxing is the national governing body.

Women's boxing was added to the Olympics at London in 2012. The American Claressa Shields won the middleweight gold there and again in 2016. That first women's event came 108 years after men's Olympic boxing began. Women had fought in amateur tournaments long before the Olympics allowed them.

AIBA faced years of problems with judging, money and leadership. In 2019 the International Olympic Committee suspended its recognition. The IOC ran the boxing events itself at Tokyo 2020, held in 2021, and at Paris 2024. AIBA had renamed itself the IBA, and in 2023 the IOC withdrew recognition. A new federation, *World Boxing*, was founded in 2023 to take its place.

an international federation founded in 2023 to govern Olympic boxing
the organization that runs one Olympic sport in one country, such as USA Boxing

lessons.title: The Lystedt Law
lessons.mainIdea: Washington's 2009 Lystedt Law was the first state law requiring a young athlete with a suspected concussion to leave play until cleared.
reading: In October 2006, Zackery Lystedt was a 13-year-old football player in Maple Valley, Washington. He hit his head during a middle school game. He went back in after a short rest. After the game he collapsed from a brain injury. He survived after emergency surgery but faced a long recovery.

A *concussion* is a brain injury caused by a blow or jolt to the head or body. It can happen in football, soccer, wrestling, judo or boxing. Doctors warn that a second blow before healing can cause much worse harm. Lystedt's family, doctors and lawyers pushed Washington lawmakers to act.

In May 2009 Governor Christine Gregoire signed the *Lystedt Law*. It had three main parts. Athletes and parents had to sign a concussion information sheet each year. An athlete with a suspected concussion had to be removed from play. Return required written clearance from a licensed health care provider trained in concussions.

Washington's 2009 youth concussion law, named for Zackery Lystedt
written permission from a health care provider to return to play

lessons.title: Illinois Concussion Rules
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois passed a youth concussion law in 2011 and expanded it in 2015 to cover returning to class as well as to play.
reading: After Washington acted, other states followed quickly. Oregon passed Max's Law in 2009, named for high school football player Max Conradt. By 2014 every state had some kind of youth concussion law. Most copied Washington's three parts: education, removal from play and written clearance.

Illinois passed its law in 2011. It required school boards to adopt concussion policies that match the rules of the Illinois High School Association. A student athlete with a suspected concussion must be removed from practice or play. The student may not return without clearance from a doctor or trained athletic trainer. The IHSA also wrote its own return-to-play policy for all its sports.

In 2015 Illinois expanded the rules with the Youth Sports Concussion Safety Act. Each school must have a *concussion oversight team* that writes a *return-to-learn* plan as well as a return-to-play plan. Return-to-learn means a student may need lighter schoolwork while the brain heals. Coaches and officials must complete concussion training.

lessons.title: Weigh-ins and Skin Checks
lessons.mainIdea: After three college wrestlers died cutting weight in 1997, wrestling rule makers added weight programs and kept skin checks at weigh-ins.
reading: Wrestlers compete in *weight classes*, so a match pairs people of similar size. For decades, some wrestlers tried to lose weight fast before a weigh-in. In late 1997, three college wrestlers died within about six weeks while trying to lose weight quickly. They wrestled in North Carolina, Wisconsin and Michigan.

The NCAA changed its rules in 1998. It moved weigh-ins closer to the start of competition. It banned rubber suits and saunas for losing weight. It also set up a weight certification program early in each season. High school rule makers soon took similar steps.

The *NFHS*, the National Federation of State High School Associations, writes the national high school wrestling rules. It was founded in Chicago in 1920. Its rules require each state to run a weight management program. That program sets a lowest allowed weight for each wrestler and limits how fast a wrestler may drop to it. At weigh-ins, officials also check skin for contagious conditions. A wrestler with a sore needs a doctor's signed form to compete.

the National Federation of State High School Associations, founded in Chicago in 1920; it writes high school rule books

lessons.title: A Studio Needs No State License
lessons.mainIdea: In most U.S. states, a martial arts studio can open without any state license to teach, so private groups set its standards.
reading: States license many jobs that touch the public. Illinois licenses barbers, nurses, electricians and professional boxing officials. In most states, though, no license is needed to teach karate, judo or taekwondo. A studio usually needs a city business license, a lease and a building that passes fire and safety codes.

Standards inside a studio come from *private* groups instead. The Kodokan in Tokyo, founded in 1882, awards judo ranks. The Kukkiwon in Seoul, opened in 1972, issues taekwondo rank certificates. National bodies such as USA Judo certify coaches and referees. A studio may join these groups, but in most places the law does not require it.

This gap matters for families. A certificate on the wall shows that a private group approved a teacher's rank. It does not show that a state checked the room or the teacher. Parents can ask whether a studio belongs to a national body, carries insurance and runs background checks. Those questions help families learn who stands behind the sign.

lessons.title: The Sports Act and National Bodies
lessons.mainIdea: The Amateur Sports Act of 1978 set up one national governing body for each Olympic sport, and those bodies set rules for their member clubs.
reading: In the 1970s, U.S. amateur sport was split among rival groups. The Amateur Athletic Union and college groups often fought over who could send athletes to international events. In 1975 President Gerald Ford created the President's Commission on Olympic Sports to study the problem. Its report led to a new federal law.

Congress passed the *Amateur Sports Act of 1978*. It made the U.S. Olympic Committee the coordinating body for Olympic sport. It let the committee recognize one national governing body for each sport. The law also protected athletes' right to compete. In 1998 Congress renamed it the Ted Stevens Olympic and Amateur Sports Act.

Today USA Judo, USA Taekwondo, USA Wrestling and USA Boxing are the national governing bodies for their sports. They register member clubs, certify coaches and referees and run national championships. Adults in these clubs must follow SafeSport rules. A club that joins a governing body accepts a rule book that reaches from the national office into its own room.

words.d: a federal law that organized U.S. Olympic sport under one national governing body per sport
a U.S. sports organization founded in 1888 that once controlled many amateur sports

review.q: How is a sanctioning body different from a state athletic commission?
choices: A sanctioning body is part of the government.
A commission ranks boxers for title fights.
A sanctioning body is private and approves title fights; a commission is a government licensing agency.
They are two names for the same group.
review.why: Sanctioning bodies like the WBC are private, while commissions are state or tribal agencies.

review.q: What gap did the Professional Boxing Safety Act of 1996 close?
choices: It let high schools hold pro bouts.
It stopped pro bouts from being held without commission supervision.
review.why: The 1996 law required a state or tribal commission to supervise every pro bout in the U.S.

review.q: Which three parts did most youth concussion laws copy from Washington?
choices: education, removal from play and written clearance
review.why: The 2009 Lystedt Law set the model of education, removal and written clearance.

review.q: What did Illinois add in 2015 that its 2011 law did not stress?
choices: return-to-learn plans and concussion oversight teams
review.why: The Youth Sports Concussion Safety Act of 2015 added return-to-learn plans and oversight teams.

review.q: Which rule maker writes the national high school wrestling rules?
review.why: The NFHS, founded in Chicago in 1920, writes high school rule books, including weight and skin rules.

review.q: In most U.S. states, who checks a martial arts teacher's rank?
choices: private groups such as the Kodokan, the Kukkiwon or USA Judo
review.why: Most states do not license martial arts teachers, so private and national bodies set rank standards.
